question.title: Cloud Run vs Cloud Functions
question.scenario: You need to run a containerized application that handles HTTP requests and requires custom system libraries. The application has complex dependencies.
question.question-text: Why might Cloud Run be preferred over Cloud Functions for this scenario?

choices.choice: Cloud Run supports any container image with any dependencies
Cloud Functions has better scaling capabilities
Cloud Run is always cheaper than Cloud Functions
Cloud Functions cannot handle HTTP requests

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Run accepts any container image you build, giving you unrestricted control over the runtime, system libraries, and dependencies, whereas Cloud Functions limits you to specific supported runtimes.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Run accepts any container image, giving you full control over the runtime environment, system-level dependencies, and installed libraries. Cloud Functions constrains you to specific supported runtimes and may not support all native system libraries your application needs. Option B is wrong because both services autoscale effectively. Option C is incorrect because pricing depends on usage patterns; Functions can be cheaper for lightweight event processing. Option D is false because Cloud Functions fully supports HTTP triggers. For applications with complex or unusual dependencies, Cloud Run's container flexibility is the decisive advantage.

ul.li: Cloud Functions 2nd gen is actually built on Cloud Run under the hood, meaning the underlying infrastructure is the same; the difference is in the developer experience and the constraints each surface imposes.

Cloud Run supports request timeouts up to 60 minutes and allows multiple concurrent requests per container instance (up to 1000), while Cloud Functions 1st gen is limited to 9-minute timeouts and processes one request at a time per instance.

Cloud Run allows you to configure CPU allocation to be always-on (charged continuously) for background processing, or request-based (charged only during request handling), giving you more control over cost and compute behavior.

Choose Cloud Functions when you want the simplest developer experience for lightweight event-driven logic; choose Cloud Run when you need container-level control, longer execution times, gRPC support, or WebSocket connections.

question.question-text: What does the GKE cluster autoscaler do in this situation?

question.title: Cloud Run Concurrency
question.scenario: Your Cloud Run service handles requests that are CPU-intensive. You want to ensure each container instance handles only one request at a time.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Run setting controls how many concurrent requests a single container instance handles?

choices.choice: Maximum instances setting
Minimum instances setting
CPU allocation setting
Container instance concurrency setting

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Run has a per-instance concurrency setting that controls how many simultaneous requests a single container instance can process, directly affecting scaling behavior and resource utilization.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Cloud Run container instance concurrency setting (configurable from 1 to 1000) determines how many requests a single container instance handles simultaneously. For CPU-intensive work, setting concurrency to 1 ensures each instance processes one request at a time, preventing resource contention. Maximum instances (A) caps total instances, not per-instance concurrency. Minimum instances (B) controls cold start mitigation. CPU allocation (C) determines when CPU is available (request-time only vs always), not request routing. Setting concurrency to 1 means Cloud Run creates a new instance for each concurrent request, trading higher instance count for predictable per-request performance.

ul.li: The default concurrency is 80; higher concurrency means fewer total instances are needed to handle the same traffic, reducing cold starts and lowering per-request cost since instance overhead is amortized across more requests.

For I/O-bound workloads (database queries, API calls, file reads), high concurrency (80-250) is optimal because the CPU is idle while waiting for I/O; for CPU-bound workloads (image processing, computation), concurrency of 1-4 prevents thread starvation.

Your application code must be thread-safe to use concurrency greater than 1; if the application uses global mutable state or non-thread-safe libraries, set concurrency to 1 to avoid race conditions and data corruption.

Cloud Run autoscaler uses the formula: target instances = concurrent requests / concurrency setting. With 100 concurrent requests and concurrency of 1, Cloud Run targets 100 instances; with concurrency of 50, it targets only 2 instances.

question.title: GKE Network Policies
question.scenario: You need to restrict network traffic between pods in your GKE cluster so that only the frontend pods can communicate with the backend pods.
question.question-text: What should you implement to control pod-to-pod network traffic?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Kubernetes Network Policies specify how groups of pods are allowed to communicate with each other and with external endpoints. They use label selectors to identify source and destination pods, defining ingress and egress rules at the pod level. VPC firewall rules (B) operate at the VM/node level and cannot distinguish between individual pods on the same node. Cloud Armor (C) protects external-facing services from DDoS and web attacks, not internal pod-to-pod traffic. IAM permissions (D) control API access to GCP resources, not network-layer pod communication. In GKE, network policies require enabling a network policy provider: either Calico or GKE Dataplane V2.

ul.li: GKE Dataplane V2 (powered by Cilium and eBPF) provides native, high-performance network policy enforcement without the overhead of iptables-based solutions like Calico, and adds built-in network policy logging for audit compliance.

By default, Kubernetes allows all pod-to-pod communication within a cluster (flat network model); once you apply any NetworkPolicy to a namespace, pods in that namespace with matching labels begin enforcing the policy, and unmatched traffic is denied.

VPC firewall rules apply at the node (VM) level using IP ranges and tags, so they cannot selectively allow frontend-pod-to-backend-pod traffic when both pod types may run on the same node, making them insufficient for fine-grained pod-level segmentation.

For defense-in-depth, combine Kubernetes Network Policies (pod-level) with VPC firewall rules (node-level) and Cloud Armor (edge-level) to create layered network security covering internal traffic, node-to-node traffic, and external-facing traffic respectively.

Option B is wrong because App Engine explicitly supports gradual traffic migration. Deploying to a different project (C) makes traffic splitting impossible without external routing. An external load balancer (D) is unnecessary because App Engine provides this capability natively. Traffic splitting is controlled via the Cloud Console, gcloud CLI, or the Admin API.

ul.li: IP-based splitting uses the hash of the client IP to route consistently to the same version, but is less accurate when users share IPs (corporate proxies, NAT); cookie-based splitting uses the GOOGAPPUID cookie for precise per-user version affinity.

Each App Engine version has a unique URL (VERSION-dot-SERVICE-dot-PROJECT.appspot.com) for direct testing before routing any production traffic, allowing QA validation of the new version without affecting live users.

App Engine supports gradual traffic migration that automatically ramps traffic to the new version over a configurable period, or manual migration where you control the exact percentage at each step of the rollout.

Traffic splitting operates at the App Engine service level (not project level), so each service (e.g., default, api, worker) can independently manage its own version rollout cadence and traffic distribution strategy.

question.title: GKE Release Channels
question.scenario: Your team wants automatic Kubernetes version upgrades while maintaining stability for production workloads.
question.question-text: Which GKE feature provides managed version upgrades with different stability levels?

choices.choice: GKE does not support automatic upgrades
Manual version pinning only
Release channels (Rapid, Regular, Stable)
Automatic upgrade to latest version immediately

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GKE offers multiple release channels that provide automatic Kubernetes version upgrades at different velocities, letting you choose between early access to new features and maximum production stability.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: GKE release channels (Rapid, Regular, Stable) provide automatic, managed Kubernetes version upgrades with different maturity levels. Rapid receives new versions first for early testing, Regular provides a balanced approach for most workloads, and Stable offers the most-tested versions with the longest validation period. Option A is false because automatic upgrades are a core GKE capability. Manual version pinning (B) is possible but is not a managed upgrade feature. Option D is incorrect because upgrades are staged through channels, not applied immediately to all clusters. Channels ensure your cluster stays on supported, security-patched versions without manual intervention.

ul.li: An Extended channel is available for customers with premium support, providing even longer support windows for stable versions, giving teams more time to validate and prepare for Kubernetes minor version upgrades.

Maintenance windows and maintenance exclusions control exactly when automatic upgrades occur (e.g., only during off-peak hours on weekdays) and when they are blocked (e.g., during holiday freezes), giving you operational control within the automated upgrade framework.

Surge upgrades minimize disruption during node pool upgrades by creating additional nodes (surge nodes) before draining and upgrading existing nodes, ensuring workload capacity is maintained throughout the upgrade process.

Node auto-upgrade (enabled by default with release channels) automatically upgrades nodes to match the control plane version, with configurable blue-green or surge strategies and respect for pod disruption budgets to maintain application availability.

question.title: Artifact Registry for Containers
question.scenario: You need a secure, private registry to store container images used by your GKE clusters and Cloud Run services.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides a managed container registry integrated with GKE and Cloud Run?

choices.choice: Cloud Source Repositories
Cloud Storage
Container Registry (deprecated)
Artifact Registry

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP's current recommended service for storing and managing container images is a universal artifact management platform that also supports language packages and integrates natively with GKE, Cloud Run, and Cloud Build.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Artifact Registry is Google Cloud's universal artifact management service and the recommended replacement for the deprecated Container Registry. It stores Docker container images, Helm charts, and language packages (Maven, npm, Python, Go), integrates with Cloud Build for CI/CD, GKE and Cloud Run for deployment, and provides vulnerability scanning. Cloud Source Repositories (A) stores source code, not container images. Cloud Storage (B) is object storage, not a container registry. Container Registry (C) is deprecated and being sunset in favor of Artifact Registry, which offers superior features including IAM-based access control, regional and multi-regional repositories, and cross-format artifact storage.

ul.li: Container Registry (gcr.io) is deprecated; Google recommends migrating to Artifact Registry, which provides the same Docker V2 API compatibility plus fine-grained IAM permissions at the repository level (instead of the bucket-level permissions gcr.io used).

Artifact Registry supports multiple artifact formats in a single service: Docker images, Helm charts, Maven/Gradle packages, npm packages, Python packages, Go modules, and APT/YUM OS packages, consolidating artifact management.

Binary Authorization integrates with Artifact Registry to enforce deploy-time policies: only container images that have been signed (attested) by trusted authorities can be deployed to GKE or Cloud Run, preventing unauthorized or unscanned images from reaching production.

Artifact Registry provides automatic vulnerability scanning powered by Container Analysis, which checks images against known CVE databases and can block deployment of images with critical vulnerabilities when combined with Binary Authorization policies.

question.title: OS Patch Management
question.scenario: You need to ensure all Compute Engine VMs are patched with the latest security updates and maintain compliance reports.
question.question-text: Which GCP service manages OS patch deployment and compliance for Compute Engine VMs?

choices.choice: Manual SSH patching only
Cloud Build
Deployment Manager
OS Patch Management (VM Manager)

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP provides a centralized fleet management service that automates OS patch deployment across Compute Engine VMs, tracks patch compliance status, and generates reports for security audits.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VM Manager (which includes OS Patch Management) automates OS patch deployment across your Compute Engine VM fleet, provides compliance reporting, and supports scheduled patch jobs for both Windows and Linux VMs. Manual SSH patching (A) does not scale and cannot provide compliance reports. Cloud Build (B) is a CI/CD service for building and testing code, not for OS-level patching. Deployment Manager (C) provisions infrastructure but does not manage ongoing OS patches. VM Manager reduces the security risk window by automating the patch lifecycle and providing visibility into which VMs are out of compliance with your patching policies.

ul.li: The OS Config agent must be installed on each VM (it comes pre-installed on most Google-provided public images); it communicates with the VM Manager service to receive patch jobs, report inventory, and execute compliance policies.

Patch jobs can be scoped using filters (by zone, label, instance name, or OS type) and configured with rollout settings (percentage-based or zone-by-zone) to control the blast radius and avoid patching all VMs simultaneously.

OS Inventory management tracks all installed packages, available updates, and Windows Update/apt/yum repository metadata across your fleet, providing a centralized view of your VM software inventory for compliance auditing and vulnerability assessment.

OS Policies (declarative configuration management) extend VM Manager beyond patching to enforce desired state: ensure specific packages are installed, files exist with expected content, or scripts have run successfully, similar to lightweight configuration management without external tools.

question.title: Compute Service Selection
question.scenario: A company needs to choose the right GCP compute service for different workloads: a stateless API, a legacy monolithic application requiring specific OS configurations, and a machine learning training pipeline.
question.question-text: What is the best mapping of workloads to compute services?

choices.choice: Cloud Run for stateless API, Compute Engine for legacy app, Vertex AI with GPUs for ML training
App Engine for all three workloads
GKE for all three workloads
Cloud Functions for all three workloads

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The best practice for GCP compute selection is matching each workload to the service that best fits its specific requirements: serverless for stateless APIs, VMs for legacy apps needing OS control, and specialized ML platforms for training pipelines.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Each workload maps to the compute service best suited for its requirements. Cloud Run handles the stateless API with automatic scaling, pay-per-use pricing, and zero server management. Compute Engine provides the full VM control and specific OS configurations the legacy monolith needs. Vertex AI with GPU/TPU support (or Compute Engine with GPUs) is purpose-built for ML training pipelines. App Engine for all three (B) cannot handle specific OS requirements or ML training efficiently. GKE for all three (C) adds unnecessary Kubernetes complexity for the API and legacy app. Cloud Functions for all three (D) cannot run a monolith or ML training pipeline within its constraints.

ul.li: The GCP compute decision tree considers four factors: management overhead (serverless to full-control), scaling model (event-driven, request-driven, or capacity-based), runtime requirements (language constraints, OS access, hardware accelerators), and cost model (pay-per-invocation, pay-per-request, or pay-per-resource-hour).

GKE is a valid choice when you need Kubernetes features (CRDs, service mesh, operators) or want to standardize on containers across diverse workloads, but it introduces significant operational complexity that should be justified by concrete Kubernetes-specific requirements.

Cloud Functions is best for lightweight, event-driven glue logic (file processing, webhook handlers, scheduled tasks) with execution times under 60 minutes and simple dependency trees; it should not be used as a general-purpose application runtime.

For ML training specifically, Vertex AI provides managed training jobs with built-in GPU/TPU support, hyperparameter tuning, experiment tracking, and integration with model serving, making it more productive than raw Compute Engine with GPUs for most ML teams.
